title: くすぶる「円安第2波」警戒論　主役は実需マネー、政策対応難しく
extracted_text:
市場参加者の間で、今年半ば以降の「円安第2波」を予想する声がくすぶっている。イラン情勢を受け、原油などのエネルギー価格上昇の影響が長引くという見立てだ。企業などの実需マネー主導の円安は為替介入などの政策対応が難しく、円安局面の長期化につながる可能性もある。

円相場の値動きが鈍い。イラン軍事衝突が始まって2カ月近くが経過したが、1ドル=158〜160円を中心にした狭い値幅での売買が続き、基軸通貨のドルに資金が退避する「有事のドル買い」の構図はさほど目立っていない。

背景にあるのは、ヘッジファンドなどの投機マネーが円売りを主導していることだ。日本政府による円買い介入への警戒感が強く、円を売った後に速やかに円を買い戻す短期売買が優勢になっている。

もっとも市場の円先安観は消えていない。市場が見据えているのは、企業などの実需マネーが主導する先行きの円売り拡大、「円安第2波」だ。イラン情勢で原油価格は一時急騰したが、いまのところ輸入価格上昇による円安は強まっていない。中東からの原油輸入が止まり、政府が原油備蓄を放出したこともあり、足元では貿易赤字が顕在化していないからだ。

だが先行きイラン情勢が落ち着き、原油輸入が再開されたとしても、イラン軍事衝突で中東の石油精製施設などは少なからず破壊されている。

野村総合研究所 の木内登英氏は「ホルムズ海峡への機雷敷設に対する警戒感もあり、中東からの原油輸送には当分の間、リスクプレミアムが加わる可能性も高い」として、原油価格が落ち着きを取り戻すまでに数カ月から半年程度の時間がかかるとみる。しかも日本企業の主要なサプライチェーン（供給網）先であるアジア地域から輸入する部品や食材などにも、原油高の影響で価格上昇圧力がかかる可能性を否めない。

原油関連の輸入価格が上昇すれば、輸入に占めるエネルギーの割合が大きい日本の貿易構造は多大な影響を受ける。13日公表のQUICK外為月次調査によると、多くの為替市場関係者が「2026年は大幅な貿易赤字になる」と見込んでいることが分かった。5兆〜15兆円の赤字を予想する意見が半数以上を占め、20兆円規模に達するという意見も少なからずあった。

振り返ると、貿易赤字が20兆円規模に達した22年もロシアによるウクライナ侵略があり、国際資源価格の上昇で円安が加速。年初の115円台から秋にかけて一時150円の節目を突き抜けた経緯がある。

市場には国際紛争と資源価格高騰という共通点から、22年の急激な円安局面を連想する声もあり、マーケット・リスク・アドバイザリーの深谷幸司氏は「イラン情勢の先行きは読みづらいが、円相場が160円の節目を抜ける展開になる可能性も十分にある」とみる。

実需マネー主導の円安が進む場合、日本政府の対応も難しさを増す。投機的な円売りが進む場合は欧米からも円買い介入への理解を得やすいが、企業行動に伴う円安の場合、円売りが加速しないかぎり、どこまで人為的に抑え込めるかは不透明だ。しかも投機マネーのように利益確定の買い戻しが前提の円売りと違い、実需マネーの円売りには買い戻しが伴わない。

これまで160円の節目を防波堤として、行き過ぎた円安をけん制してきた日本政府。仮にイラン情勢が収束に向かっても、実需マネーへの警戒は残る。政府と市場の1ドル=160円を巡る攻防は長期戦になる可能性も否めない。

（編集委員　小栗太）

translated_text: Among market participants, voices predicting a 'second wave of yen depreciation' from mid-year onwards are growing. The assessment is that the impact of rising energy prices such as crude oil due to the Iran situation will persist. Yen depreciation led by real-demand money from companies makes policy responses such as currency intervention difficult, and could also lead to prolonged yen depreciation. The yen's exchange rate movements have been sluggish. Since the Iranian military conflict began nearly two months ago, trading has continued in a narrow range centered around ¥158-160 per dollar, and the 'safe-haven dollar buying' pattern where funds retreat to the benchmark currency dollar hasn't been particularly prominent. The background is that speculative money from hedge funds is leading the yen selling. There is strong vigilance about the Japanese government's yen-buying intervention, and short-term trades that quickly buy back yen after selling it are dominant. However, the market's view that the yen will weaken further has not disappeared. What the market is anticipating is the expansion of future yen sales led by real-demand money from companies, the 'second wave of yen depreciation.' While crude oil prices temporarily spiked due to the Iran situation, yen depreciation driven by rising import prices has not intensified for now. This is because crude oil imports from the Middle East have halted, and the government has released strategic oil reserves, so a trade deficit has not yet emerged. However, even if the Iran situation calms down and crude oil imports resume, Middle Eastern petroleum refining facilities and others were considerably damaged in the Iranian military conflict. Wood Nobuhide of Nomura Research Institute says, 'There is also vigilance about the threat of mine-laying in the Strait of Hormuz, and it is highly likely that a risk premium will be added to crude oil transport from the Middle East for the time being.' He believes it will take several months to half a year for crude oil prices to stabilize. Moreover, the possibility of rising price pressures on parts and food materials imported from Asia, which are major supply chain sources for Japanese companies, cannot be ruled out due to high crude oil prices. If crude oil-related import prices rise, Japan's trade structure, where energy makes up a large proportion of imports, will be greatly affected. According to the QUICK monthly FX survey released on the 13th, many foreign exchange market participants were found to expect '2026 will see a significant trade deficit.' Opinions forecasting deficits of 5-15 trillion yen accounted for more than half, and there were quite a few opinions that it could reach the 20 trillion yen scale. Looking back, 2022, when the trade deficit reached the 20 trillion yen scale, also saw Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and yen depreciation accelerated due to rising international resource prices. It temporarily broke through the 150 yen level from around 115 yen at the start of the year toward autumn. In the market, there are also voices recalling the rapid yen depreciation phase of 2022 due to the common factors of international conflicts and high resource prices. Market Risk Advisory's Fukaya Koji says, 'While the future direction of the Iran situation is difficult to read, there is also sufficient possibility that the yen exchange rate could break through the 160 yen level.' If real-demand-driven yen depreciation proceeds, the Japanese government's response will also become more difficult. When speculative yen selling progresses, understanding for yen-buying intervention can be obtained from the US and Europe, but in the case of yen depreciation accompanying corporate actions, it is unclear how much can be artificially restrained unless yen selling accelerates. Moreover, unlike speculative yen selling, which presupposes buybacks for profit-taking, real-demand yen selling does not involve buybacks. Until now, the Japanese government has used the 160 yen level as a breakwater to check excessive yen depreciation. Even if the Iran situation heads toward resolution, vigilance toward real-demand money will remain. It cannot be denied that the battle with the market over the 1 dollar = 160 yen level could become a prolonged struggle.
title_en: Warning of 'second wave of yen depreciation' brewing: real-demand money as main player, policy response difficult
